article.headline: Tower Semiconductor's Hybrid-Bonded Photonics Claims a 2× Bandwidth Lead
article.lede: A technical chart circulating among optical-semiconductor investors distills the central competition in silicon photonics foundry services to a single figure: 110 gigahertz versus 46. The gap marks the difference between modulator technology that can carry the next generation of AI-datacenter traffic and technology that cannot.
article.body:
The chart, shared by engineering analyst @insane_analyst, plots the *electro-optical frequency response* — the *S21 parameter* — of silicon photonics modulators fabricated on three different integration platforms: two using hybrid bonding and one using a conventional monolithic approach. A modulator's 3 dB *EO bandwidth* is the frequency at which its optical output falls to half its low-frequency power when driven electrically; it sets the hard ceiling on per-lane data rate. At 46.6 GHz, the monolithic platform tops out at 100 gigabits per second per lane under *PAM4* modulation — the 800G pluggable transceiver generation. At 110 GHz, a hybrid-bonded modulator clears the 200G-per-lane threshold needed for 1.6 terabit transceivers.

The difference comes down to how the *photonic integrated circuit* (PIC) — the chip that actually modulates light — is connected to the *electronic integrated circuit* (EIC) that drives it. In a monolithic design, both are built on the same wafer in a single process flow, keeping interconnects short but forcing a compromise between the doping profiles CMOS electronics demand and the low-absorption waveguide geometries photonics requires. **Hybrid bonding** resolves the tradeoff by fabricating the two dies separately and pressing them face-to-face in a wafer-level bond, creating copper-to-copper interconnects at sub-micron pitch with no solder bumps. The *RC parasitics* — the resistance-capacitance time constants that bleed away high-frequency signal — collapse, and modulator bandwidth roughly doubles.

**Tower Semiconductor (TSEM)** has industrialized hybrid bonding at 300mm scale by repurposing process knowledge from its image-sensor lines, where backside-illuminated stacked sensors required the same face-to-face bonding geometry. The company demonstrated 420 gigabits-per-second PAM4 transmission with Coherent (COHR) at OFC 2026 and claims $1.3 billion in signed silicon photonics contracts for 2027, with a five-fold capacity expansion under way. GlobalFoundries (GFS), whose GF Fotonix platform is the leading commercial monolithic silicon photonics process, acquired Advanced Micro Foundry in late 2025 to bolster its *O-band* capabilities and is building its own hybrid bonding path — but the data in this chart suggests that path has not yet closed the bandwidth gap.

The O-band table in the image — measurements taken at 1310 nm wavelengths where chromatic dispersion in standard single-mode fiber approaches zero — shows modulator bandwidth ranging from 40 GHz to 81 GHz across operating points, alongside *extinction ratio* (ER), *insertion loss* (IL), and *optical modulation amplitude* (OMA) figures. The bandwidth variation with wavelength and bias voltage is normal; modulators are tuned to a three-way trade-off between speed, drive voltage, and signal quality. What the table makes plain is that even the best operating points of the lower-tier platform fall short of the roughly 100 GHz floor the 1.6T standard demands.

The investment argument embedded in the chart is not subtle. Hyperscalers are in active 800G deployment and placing early orders for 1.6T transceivers. Nvidia (NVDA), which is transitioning its switch interconnects to *co-packaged optics* — where the optical engine sits directly on the switch ASIC package rather than in a pluggable cage — has been identified in Irrational Analysis coverage as a Tower customer for ring-modulator-based silicon photonics. A 2.4× bandwidth advantage, demonstrated in a production-ready process, is the kind of structural moat that shifts foundry-selection decisions for a decade-long technology buildout.

concepts.definition: A device that converts an electrical signal into a change in the intensity or phase of a light beam. In silicon photonics transceivers, an EO modulator encodes digital data onto a laser carrier by rapidly switching the optical output on and off at tens to hundreds of gigahertz.

A scattering (S) parameter that measures how much signal power travels from port 1 (the electrical input) to port 2 (the optical output). In EO modulator characterization, the S21 curve plotted versus frequency shows how efficiently high-frequency electrical signals are converted into optical modulation; the 3 dB point is where that efficiency drops by half, defining the modulator's usable bandwidth.

The electro-optical 3 dB bandwidth of a modulator — the frequency at which the optical modulation depth falls to half its low-frequency value. Higher bandwidth allows encoding more data per second; roughly 100 GHz or above is needed for 200 Gbaud (200G per lane) operation required by 1.6T optical transceivers.

A wafer-level 3D integration technique that presses two chip dies face-to-face and forms direct copper-to-copper metal interconnects at sub-micron pitch, with no solder bumps or wire bonds. Originally developed for stacked image sensors, it is now applied in photonics to connect a PIC to an EIC with ultra-short, low-parasitic interconnects that enable very high modulator bandwidth.

A fabrication approach in which photonic devices and CMOS transistors are all built on the same wafer in one continuous process flow. It simplifies assembly and lowers cost but forces a performance compromise, since the ideal process conditions for electronics and photonics conflict — limiting achievable EO bandwidth.

A technology platform that builds photonic devices — modulators, waveguides, photodetectors — using silicon and related materials on standard semiconductor wafers, leveraging existing CMOS manufacturing infrastructure. It is the dominant platform for high-volume datacom transceivers because of its low cost and scalability.

Pulse Amplitude Modulation with 4 levels — a signalling scheme that encodes 2 bits per symbol by using four distinct signal amplitudes instead of the two used in simpler NRZ signalling. At a given baud rate, PAM4 doubles data throughput, but it is more sensitive to noise and requires tighter modulator linearity and higher bandwidth. It is the standard for 100G/lane and 200G/lane optical transceivers.

The Original band of optical fiber transmission, centered near 1310 nm wavelength. Chromatic dispersion — the frequency-dependent spreading of optical pulses — is near zero in standard single-mode fiber at this wavelength, making the O-band preferred for short-reach datacenter links where dispersion compensation would otherwise add cost and complexity.

Unintentional resistance (R) and capacitance (C) in an electrical circuit — here, the interconnect between an electronic driver and a photonic modulator. RC parasitics act as a low-pass filter, rolling off high-frequency signal amplitude and setting a practical ceiling on modulator bandwidth independent of the modulator's intrinsic physics.

The ratio of the optical power in the ON state to the power in the OFF state of a modulator, expressed in dB. A higher extinction ratio means a cleaner on/off distinction, reducing bit errors at the receiver. Silicon photonics modulators typically achieve 3–6 dB extinction ratio.

The optical power lost as a signal passes through a device in its on (transmitting) state, expressed in dB. Lower insertion loss means more optical power reaches the receiver, enabling longer reach or relaxed laser power requirements. Silicon photonics modulators typically incur 1–5 dB insertion loss.

The difference in optical power between the high and low levels of a modulated optical signal, expressed in mW or dBm. OMA directly determines how easily a receiver can distinguish ones from zeros; standards bodies specify minimum OMA values for compliant transceivers.

A chip that contains multiple photonic components — waveguides, modulators, splitters, photodetectors — on a single substrate. In optical transceiver design, the PIC handles all light-routing and modulation functions.

In the context of silicon photonics transceivers, the driver and transimpedance amplifier chip that provides electrical signals to drive the PIC's modulators and amplify its photodetector outputs. The electrical interface between EIC and PIC is the bandwidth bottleneck that hybrid bonding directly addresses.

A packaging approach in which optical transceivers are integrated directly onto the same package substrate as a switch ASIC or GPU, rather than in separate pluggable modules connected by a long electrical SerDes lane. CPO eliminates a power-hungry electrical link, reducing latency and power consumption for the highest-bandwidth AI-cluster interconnects.

ticker_tsem.name: Tower Semiconductor
ticker_tsem.blurb: Tower Semiconductor is an Israeli specialty foundry that fabricates analogue, mixed-signal, and photonic chips across 200mm and 300mm wafer lines. Unlike pure-play logic foundries such as TSMC, Tower focuses on differentiated process technologies where customers need more than commodity nodes — silicon photonics, silicon-germanium (SiGe), radio-frequency CMOS, and power management. Tower's silicon photonics platform (SiPho) is widely regarded as one of the most mature independent photonics foundry offerings, supporting both passive waveguide structures and active electro-optic components on the same wafer. The company operates fabs in Israel, the United States, Japan, and Italy.
ticker_tsem.recent: Tower committed $920 million in capital expenditure to silicon photonics and SiGe capacity — a 40% increase from a plan announced just three months earlier — with over 70% of that reserved or prepaid by customers through 2028. In November 2025, the company launched a dedicated CPO Foundry offering with 300mm wafer-bonding technology and targeted more than quintupling its monthly SiPho wafer shipments between Q4 2025 and late 2026. In March 2026, Tower announced full ownership of its 300mm Fab 7 facility in Japan to support this expansion, positioning itself to challenge GlobalFoundries for the top-ranked independent silicon photonics foundry slot.

ticker_gfs.name: GlobalFoundries Inc.
ticker_gfs.blurb: GlobalFoundries Inc. (NASDAQ: GFS) is the world's third-largest semiconductor foundry by revenue, operating advanced manufacturing facilities in the United States (Fab 8 in Malta, NY; Vermont), Germany (Dresden), and Singapore. Unlike TSMC and Samsung, GlobalFoundries exited the leading-edge node race in 2018 and now focuses on differentiated specialty processes: silicon photonics, silicon-germanium (SiGe), RF CMOS, FD-SOI (fully depleted silicon-on-insulator), and embedded non-volatile memory. This positions GF as a complement — and sometimes a competitor — to Tower Semiconductor in the specialty foundry space.
ticker_gfs.recent: GF reported FY2025 revenue of $6.79 billion (up 1% year-over-year) with gross margin improving 360 basis points to 29% and diluted EPS of $1.72. Silicon photonics revenue exceeded $200 million in 2025 and is expected to nearly double in 2026, with management guiding toward a $1 billion annual run rate by end-2028. In June 2025, the company announced a $16 billion US investment plan anchored by its New York and Vermont fabs. GF also finalised a $1.5 billion CHIPS Act direct-funding agreement with the US government. In January 2026, GF agreed to acquire Synopsys' ARC Processor IP unit, targeting physical-AI embedded applications.

ticker_cohr.name: Coherent Corp.
ticker_cohr.blurb: Coherent Corp. (formerly II-VI Incorporated, rebranded after the 2022 acquisition of Lumentum rival Coherent) develops and manufactures engineered materials, optoelectronic components, and laser systems across three segments: Networking, Materials, and Lasers. Its Networking segment — the primary AI data-center play — supplies indium-phosphide chips, transceiver modules, and silicon-photonics sub-assemblies to hyperscalers and networking OEMs. With roughly $5.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, it is one of the largest vertically integrated photonics companies in the world.
ticker_cohr.recent: Coherent joined the S&P 500 in March 2026, the same month it announced general availability of the industry's first dual-laser QSFP28-DCO module — a compact form factor enabling 100G coherent transmission over a single fiber with up to 300 km reach. At OFC 2026 the company showcased an expanded InP portfolio including 400 mW CW lasers, 200G/400G photodiodes, and 800G/1.6T modulators. Fifteen analysts hold an average "Strong Buy" rating with a consensus 12-month price target near $278.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.
